extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP attorneys, in-house counsel and practitioners handling design patent infringement matters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating design patent infringement after Egyptian Goddess, focusing on the revised ordinary-observer test, the role of prior art, and the 'plainly dissimilar' threshold as applied in subsequent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test (through eyes familiar with the prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate analysis is an 'ordinary observer test through the eyes of an observer familiar with the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior-art-aware ordinary observer is now the governing perspective after Egyptian Goddess. Consideration of prior art is not required in every case, only those in which the patented design and the accused design are 'substantially the same.' Use this observer standard when determining substantial similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of the 'point of novelty' test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit rejected the 'point of novelty' test, which required that the accused design contain 'substantially the same points of novelty that distinguished the patented design from the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not analyze infringement by focusing solely on whether the accused design appropriated a single specified feature or point of novelty; the inquiry should address whether the accused design appropriates the claimed design as a whole. Courts should avoid isolating a single feature to the exclusion of the overall design comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Plainly dissimilar' threshold / two-level analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the two designs are not 'plainly dissimilar,' the infringement analysis 'will benefit from a comparison of the claimed and accused designs with the prior art.' Some courts treat this as a two-level process: a level-one 'threshold' analysis to decide if prior-art comparison is necessary, and a level-two analysis that accounts for prior art in less obvious cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First assess whether the accused and claimed designs are plainly dissimilar (if they are, prior-art comparison may not be necessary). If they are not plainly dissimilar, proceed to compare both designs to relevant prior art to provide context. Cases: Wing Shing, Minka, Keurig provide examples of applying the two levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial overall visual impression (would an ordinary observer find designs substantially the same?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the patented design and the accused product 'in the eye[s] of an ordinary observer, giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives' and determine whether the 'two designs [were] substantially the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the overall visual impression rather than immediately dissecting individual features. If the overall impressions are not substantially the same, the infringement claim is weak; if they appear substantially the same, move to finer-grained analysis and possibly prior-art comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare claimed and accused designs to prior art for context
rubrics_metrics.description: In situations where designs are not plainly dissimilar (or where the field is crowded), courts should compare the claimed and accused designs with the prior art to provide a reference point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior art as a 'concrete guidepost' and context for what features are common to the field. Wing Shing illustrates extensive prior-art comparison leading to a finding of non-infringement because the field was 'crowded with many references.' Prior-art comparison can show that ostensibly similar features are common and not distinctive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether similarities/differences are ornamental or functional
rubrics_metrics.description: When dissecting similarities and differences, courts may designate each and every similarity and difference as being ornamental or functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Keurig example: in a detailed side-by-side analysis, identify specific features (e.g., silhouette, finial, ornamentation, central body, contours) and decide whether each feature is ornamental (relevant to design patent analysis) or functional (less relevant to design-patent infringement). This classification affects whether a feature contributes to an ordinary observer's perception of sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdedness of the pertinent art influences the need for prior-art comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether prior art is considered appears to be a function of the level of similarity between the designs, the crowded or uncrowded nature of the pertinent art, and the court's approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a 'cluttered' field with many similar prior art references, courts are more likely to consult prior art to determine whether an ordinary observer would be deceived. If many similar designs exist, even noticeable differences may not prevent a finding that an ordinary observer familiar with the prior art would see the designs as distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the ordinary observer would be deceived/confused
rubrics_metrics.description: The core inquiry is whether the ordinary observer would believe the accused design to be the 'same as' the patented design (i.e., be deceived or confused).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the likelihood of deception from the perspective of the ordinary observer (potentially familiar with prior art). Courts evaluate whether an ordinary purchaser would be confused as to source or origin based on overall impression and contextual prior-art knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of summary judgment when designs are plainly dissimilar
rubrics_metrics.description: When courts conclude the patented design and the accused product are plainly dissimilar, they may grant summary judgment of non-infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Minka and Keurig demonstrate courts entering summary judgment where differences were sufficient that no reasonable ordinary observer would find the designs substantially the same. Use clear visual-distinction findings to support early disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial variability/conscientiousness affects the analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which prior art is used and how detailed the analysis is can depend on the conscientious nature of a particular court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect variability in outcomes and thoroughness between courts. Some judges will proceed to extensive prior-art comparisons even when they initially find designs distinguishable; others will stop at the threshold finding. Practitioners should be prepared for both approaches and tailor arguments/evidence accordingly.
